title: FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc.
lead: A change in broadcast-indecency enforcement reaches the Supreme Court after the FCC finds two awards-show broadcasts indecent but imposes no penalties.

actors.name: Federal Communications Commission
actors.role: Agency defending its changed indecency policy and administrative findings.

actors.name: Fox Television Stations and other broadcasters
actors.role: Parties challenging the findings and the agency’s explanation.

actors.name: Cher and Nicole Richie
actors.role: Performers whose broadcast words prompted complaints; not parties subjected to personal liability here.

proceedings: The FCC issued findings in 2006, then obtained a voluntary remand to consider broadcaster objections.
The Second Circuit set aside the resulting Remand Order under the APA.
The Supreme Court reversed that APA judgment and remanded without deciding the constitutional challenges.
limits: This account concerns the 2009 decision and uses the reviewed brief, including its account of the separate writings and assigned editorial notes. No Fox forfeiture was imposed. The subsequent 2010 and 2012 proceedings are editorial subsequent history, not part of this judgment or a new independent audit.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The agency develops a restrained policy for broadcast expletives
sections.cue: What regulatory practice existed before the disputed broadcasts?
paragraphs: Federal law prohibited obscene, indecent, or profane radio communications. The Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC’s) operative broadcast-indecency restrictions ran from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; litigation explained the difference between that endpoint and the statute’s broader midnight wording. The agency treated patently offensive descriptions of sexual or excretory organs or activities as indecent when children could be listening. Its contextual inquiry considered explicitness, repetition or dwelling on the material, and whether a presentation pandered, titillated, or shocked.

After the Supreme Court’s earlier broadcast-indecency decision, FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, the Commission generally separated literal descriptions from nonliteral expletives and required repetition before treating expletives as actionable. That policy supplied the background against which the television broadcaster Fox broadcast the Billboard Music Awards in 2002 and 2003. Cher used an expletive against her critics during the first broadcast. Nicole Richie used an excretory reference and an expletive in an exchange with Paris Hilton during the second. The performers’ speech generated regulatory proceedings against broadcasters; neither performer was being held personally liable in this review.

sections.title: The Golden Globes order changes the policy
sections.cue: How did the FCC address isolated words and notice?
paragraphs: In 2004, after the two Fox broadcasts, the FCC considered Bono’s use of an expletive as an intensifier on NBC’s Golden Globes broadcast. The Commission rejected the categorical protection that fleeting expletives had received. It reasoned that the word’s offensive force derived from its sexual meaning, that even isolated use could be patently offensive, and that automatic immunity might encourage more such broadcasts. Improved delay technology also made screening easier.

The Golden Globes Order acknowledged and disavowed contrary staff decisions and earlier Commission statements. The FCC declined to penalize NBC because the former policy had not supplied adequate notice. This order was the policy background for the Fox dispute; it was not one of the two awards-show broadcasts directly under review.

sections.title: The FCC hears objections and retains the Fox findings
sections.cue: Distinguish the administrative remand from the Supreme Court’s later remand.
paragraphs: A 2006 FCC order addressed several broadcasts, including Fox’s two Billboard programs. The broadcasters sought review in the Second Circuit. Because no sanctions had been imposed, they had not previously had an opportunity to respond to the particular findings. The Commission obtained a voluntary remand to hear their objections, then issued a Remand Order retaining both Fox indecency findings without a forfeiture or other sanction.

The agency emphasized the gratuitous, shocking language, the entertainment setting, and the substantial audience of children. It argued that aspects of the broadcasts violated even its former policy but used the new policy to eliminate doubt. Under that policy, lack of repetition counted against an indecency finding without automatically defeating one.

Fox and the other participants renewed their challenge. The Second Circuit majority set aside the orders because the FCC had inadequately explained its departure from its previous policy. It expressed constitutional doubts but did not decide the constitutional objections. Judge Leval dissented. The Supreme Court accepted review of the administrative-law explanation question.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural History; Material Facts; 556 U.S. at 510–513

sections.title: Five Justices find the policy change adequately explained
sections.cue: What must an agency explain when it changes course?
paragraphs: Justice Scalia wrote the controlling portions of the Supreme Court’s opinion for himself, Chief Justice Roberts, and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito. The Court applied the ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious standard under § 706(2)(A) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). An agency must acknowledge a change, remain within its authority, and offer good reasons for the new approach. It need not persuade judges that its new reasons are better than the reasons for its old policy. The Court read State Farm’s comparison as addressing rescission versus a failure to act initially, not as imposing heightened review on every policy revision; the distinct functions of § 706(1) and § 706(2) supported that reading.

Continuity nevertheless could demand additional explanation. An agency must confront contrary earlier factual findings and serious reliance interests when they matter. A changed factual or reliance setting can therefore require a more detailed explanation under the same legal standard. The Court did not authorize silent or unexplained inconsistency.

The FCC had expressly rejected its earlier positions, relied on the Golden Globes Order, and withheld penalties. Those steps acknowledged the change. Its alternative contention that Cher’s broadcast violated the former approach might be unconvincing, but the Court found it unnecessary because the new policy was independently explained. The agency could rationally connect the offensive force of the words with sexual meaning and assess a single use in context. It could also predict that categorical immunity would encourage further use and regard improved screening technology as reducing the burden of prevention.

The Court declined to demand unrealistic controlled studies of children’s exposure to broadcast profanity. It permitted predictive judgment based on children’s tendency to imitate and Congress’s regulatory judgment; it did not excuse failure to consider relevant, reasonably obtainable evidence. Nor did the policy condemn every appearance of a particular word. The agency could distinguish an awards show drawing children from other contexts, including the film example discussed in the opinion. Pacifica’s narrow holding had left questions open rather than forbidding every incremental expansion of agency policy.

sources.pinpoint: Rule and Holding; Reasoning; 556 U.S. at 513–522

sections.title: The Justices separate constitutional review from administrative explanation
sections.cue: Which portions commanded five votes, and what did the concurrences add?
paragraphs: The Court refused to use constitutional avoidance to impose a specially stringent APA explanation standard. Interpreting an ambiguous statute and asking an agency to reconsider policy because of constitutional doubts were different inquiries. Actual constitutional objections remained available directly, and the Second Circuit had not decided them.

Scalia’s Part III-E attracted only Roberts, Thomas, and Alito in addition to himself. Its discussion of congressional pressure, independent agencies, and some local-broadcaster concerns therefore had four votes. That portion recounted two 2004 congressional oversight hearings followed by the Golden Globes Order. It distinguished committee oversight wishes from enacted congressional intent, noted Congress’s exclusion from the APA, recognized that oversight cannot expand statutory authority, and resisted importing every notice-and-comment requirement into review of an adjudication. It did not establish a majority holding that political pressure alone provides lawful agency reasons.

Kennedy concurred in part and in the judgment. He emphasized rational, neutral principles, the statutory mandate, available data and experience, and serious consideration of earlier factual findings. Agreeing with Breyer that an agency sometimes must explain rejection of considerations supporting its original policy, he distinguished State Farm because the FCC’s earlier approach rested on a reading of Pacifica rather than contrary industry findings. He found the explanation adequate, though not exemplary, and joined the reservation of constitutional issues.

Thomas also concurred. He questioned the constitutional foundations and technological assumptions of Red Lion and Pacifica, including scarcity, broadcasting’s special reach, and changed parental-blocking technology. He was willing to reconsider those precedents in an appropriate case, but his concurrence did not overrule them or decide the constitutional challenge here.

sources.pinpoint: Separate Opinions; Full-opinion footnotes; 556 U.S. at 522–539

sections.title: The dissenters would require the FCC to reconsider
sections.cue: What important considerations did they believe the agency had left unanswered?
paragraphs: Breyer dissented, joined by Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg. He described his position as ordinary reasoned-decisionmaking review applied to the circumstances of a reversal. In his view, the FCC had failed to confront both the constitutional caution behind its former reading of Pacifica and the effects on local stations unable to afford delay systems. Restating concerns about offensive language and children did not explain why the prior balance should change. He did not demand controlled studies in every case; he wanted attention to existing evidence and previously recognized considerations.

The four-vote portion of Scalia’s opinion regarded local stations’ risks as overstated and the contextual safeguards as sufficient. Breyer replied that there was no categorical news exemption and that possible equitable treatment did not clearly protect stations unable to purchase equipment. These competing assessments were predictions about regulatory risk, not findings that particular small stations would violate the policy. The large possible fines discussed by the dissent were not fines imposed on Fox.

Breyer also objected under Chenery to the Solicitor General’s reliance on the statutory word “any,” a rationale supplied by litigation counsel rather than the agency. His alternative constitutional-avoidance approach would remand for agency reconsideration; it would not immediately declare the whole regime unconstitutional.

Stevens separately stressed agency independence, stability, and the distinction between an emotional expletive and an actual sexual or excretory description. He disputed the FCC’s interpretation of Pacifica, its reliance on oversight hearings, and the claimed case for broader regulation despite technological changes. Ginsburg separately emphasized the First Amendment stakes and the difference between Pacifica’s repeated monologue and fleeting emotional expression. Words offensive to some people, she stressed, may be ordinary expression to others. Both joined Breyer and would affirm the Second Circuit.

sources.pinpoint: Separate Opinions; Full-opinion footnotes; 556 U.S. at 539–567

sections.title: The Court reverses the APA judgment and leaves constitutional issues open
sections.cue: State the result without turning it into approval of every application of the policy.
paragraphs: The Supreme Court reversed the Second Circuit and remanded for further proceedings. Fox lost its claim that the agency had inadequately explained the changed policy. No payment was ordered, and the decision did not finally sustain the challenged orders against the constitutional objections reserved for further litigation.

The assigned notes place that result in a broader sequence. Their subsequent-history account describes a 2010 Second Circuit vagueness ruling and the Supreme Court’s 2012 as-applied lack-of-notice decision, while leaving the broader First Amendment issue open. Their comparisons with Modesto Irrigation, Westar Energy, Philip Morris, Dillmon, and National Association of Home Builders stress an acknowledged, reasoned departure. Discussion of Sierra Club v. Costle, Mashaw, and Metzger explores political influence and constitutional considerations; those are editorial or scholarly comparisons, not additional holdings of Fox. The notes also question where reviewing reasoning ends and substituting a judicial policy balance begins.

The later DACA discussion links Fox’s reliance principle with State Farm’s alternatives inquiry and Chenery’s bar on post hoc reasons. It describes Regents’ concerns with forbearance, benefits, structured review, and reliance; separately attributes Thomas’s illegality objection, Kavanaugh’s treatment of Nielsen’s explanation, and Sotomayor’s equal-protection position; and is not a new audit of Regents. The 2009 case itself ends with reversal on the APA explanation issue and a remand on the still-open questions.
